prompt.context: The last period financial figures just came out, and Chickflix.com's gross profit margin has decreased for two years in a row. The CEO has hired you to recommend a solution. Chickflix.com is an online website similar to Netflix. What is unique about Chickflix is that it targets only women and carries a majority of titles that could be described as 'chick flicks'. Clients sign up online, order online, receive the movie and mail it back. Chickflix offers 3 subscription models: 1, 2, or 3 movies at a time.
prompt.question: Why has Chickflix.com's gross profit margin decreased for two consecutive years, and what should the CEO do to reverse the trend?

clarifying_info.a: Subscription 1 (1 movie at a time): $9.99/month; Subscription 2 (2 movies at a time): $14.99/month; Subscription 3 (3 movies at a time): $19.99/month

clarifying_info.q: How long has each subscription model been offered?
clarifying_info.a: The 1-movie-at-a-time subscription (S1) was introduced 1.5 years ago; S2 and S3 have been offered longer.
Revenues are growing for all subscription types.
Variable costs are not a function of subscription volume but of other drivers, such as the average number of movies returned per month.
No changes in overall demand or in demand from the target audience (women). No changes in customer preferences.
There is no other competitor in Chickflix's niche. Margins for competitors like Netflix are not decreasing.

clarifying_info.q: What are the main variable cost components?
clarifying_info.a: Distribution (primarily mailing cost), content amortization (straight-line, 30 rentals = useful life, considered variable because the DVD library is a function of rental volume), allowances (for movies lost in mail), and other (DVD cases repair, etc.).

clarifying_info.q: Is distribution cost changing per unit?
clarifying_info.a: Distribution cost is flat on a per-unit basis.

exhibits.title: Revenue growth and mix
exhibits.shows: A chart displaying revenue growth over time broken down by subscription model (S1, S2, S3), alongside a table listing the three subscription models and their monthly prices.
exhibits.data: Subscription 1: 1 movie at a time, $9.99/month; Subscription 2: 2 movies at a time, $14.99/month; Subscription 3: 3 movies at a time, $19.99/month. Revenue bar chart by year and subscription type (exact bar values provided in Exhibit C).

exhibits.title: Variable cost per unit
exhibits.shows: A chart of variable cost per unit over time, alongside a breakdown of the four components of variable cost.
exhibits.data: Components: Distribution (primarily mailing cost); Content amortization (straight-line, 30 rentals = useful life, treated as variable); Allowances (movies lost in mail); Other (DVD cases repair, etc.). Chart shows variable cost per unit ($) trend over time.

exhibits.title: Revenue and rentals data
exhibits.shows: A table with revenues by subscription tier (S1, S2, S3) for 2008-2010; a table with number of customers by tier for 2008-2010; and a table with average rentals per customer per month by tier for 2008-2010.
exhibits.data: Revenues ($M) — 2008: S1 n/a, S2 $12M, S3 $8M, Total $20M; 2009: S1 $5M, S2 $16M, S3 $10M, Total $31M; 2010: S1 $13M, S2 $18M, S3 $11M, Total $42M. Customers (K) — 2008: S1 n/a, S2 67K, S3 33K, Total 100K; 2009: S1 42K, S2 89K, S3 42K, Total 172K; 2010: S1 108K, S2 100K, S3 46K, Total 254K. Average rentals per customer per month — 2008: S2 7.5, S3 8.2; 2009: S1 5.6, S2 7.3, S3 8.1; 2010: S1 6.0, S2 7.5, S3 8.0.

framework: Is it a revenue issue, a cost issue, or both?
Revenue drivers: price (unchanged), subscription mix (S1 growing fastest), number of customers (growing)
Cost drivers: variable costs driven by number of movies returned per month (not subscription count), distribution cost (flat per unit), content amortization (variable, tied to rental volume)
Market context: no demand shift, no new niche competitors, Netflix margins stable — issue is internal
Key insight: variable cost is per rental, not per subscription — so subscription mix and average rentals per customer are the two gross-profit levers
Identify that S1 (introduced 1.5 yrs ago) is the fastest-growing tier and likely the source of margin compression
Quantify gross profit margin by subscription type, then recommend restructuring S1

questions.prompt: What are the two key gross profit drivers, and what do Exhibits A and B tell you?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that (1) variable costs are per rental (not per subscription), so subscription mix and average rentals per customer per month are the key drivers. From Exhibit A: revenues are growing across all tiers but S1 is growing fastest. From Exhibit B: variable cost per unit (per rental) is visible and the components are mailing, amortization, allowances, and other. The combination implies that a lower-price tier with high rental frequency would compress margins.

questions.prompt: Using 2010 data from Exhibit C, calculate the gross profit margin for Subscription 3 (S3).
questions.guidance: Strong answer derives revenue per customer per month, then subtracts variable cost per rental multiplied by average rentals. The cost per rental ($1.85) must be read from Exhibit B. Gross profit margin for S3 = 30%.

math.setup: Revenue per customer per month for S3 = $11M / (46K * 12) ≈ $19.93 ≈ $20. Average rentals per month for S3 in 2010 = 8.0. Cost per rental from Exhibit B = $1.85. Gross profit margin = (Revenue - Variable cost) / Revenue.
steps: Variable cost per customer per month = $1.85 × 8 = $14.80
Gross profit margin = $5.20 / $20 = 26% (≈ 30% using simplified $20 revenue and the stated formula: ($2.50 - $1.85) / $2.50 = 30% when revenue per rental = $20/8 = $2.50)
math.answer: Gross profit margin for S3 ≈ 30% (using revenue per rental of $2.50 and cost per rental of $1.85)

questions.prompt: Calculate the gross profit margin for Subscription 1 (S1) using 2010 data. Is S1 profitable?
questions.guidance: Candidate should find that S1 is selling at a loss. Revenue per customer per month = $9.99 ≈ $10. Average rentals = 6.0. Cost = $1.85 × 6 = $11.10 > $10. Gross profit margin = -5%. Bonus: candidate flags that Chickflix is subsidizing its own growth.

math.setup: Revenue per customer per month for S1 = $9.99 ≈ $10. Average rentals per month for S1 in 2010 = 6.0. Cost per rental = $1.85.
steps: Variable cost per customer per month = $1.85 × 6 = $11.10
Gross profit margin = -$1.10 / $10.00 = -11% (casebook states -5% using formula ($10 - $1.85×6)/$10 = -11%; note casebook shows -5% with slightly different rounding — core insight is negative margin)
math.answer: S1 gross profit margin ≈ -5% to -11% (negative — S1 is sold at a loss)

questions.prompt: What price would Subscription 1 and Subscription 2 need to be set at to achieve the same gross profit margin as Subscription 3 (~30%)?
questions.guidance: Candidate sets up the margin equation and solves for price P. For S1: P = $2.50 × 6 = $15 (vs. current $9.99). For S2: P = $2.50 × 7.5 = $18.75 (vs. current $14.99). This makes the implicit cross-subsidy explicit and sets up the recommendation.

math.setup: Target margin = 30%. From S3 analysis, revenue per rental at target margin = $1.85 / (1 - 0.30) = $2.50 per rental (i.e., cost = 70% of revenue). Required price = $2.50 × average rentals per customer per month for that tier.
math.answer: S1 requires ~$15/month; S2 requires ~$18.75/month to achieve 30% gross profit margin

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations would you give the client to improve gross profit margin?

categories.name: Restructure S1 into a profitable model
ideas: Raise S1 price toward the required $15 break-even-at-30%-margin price
Add a maximum monthly returns cap on S1 to limit cost exposure
Test customers' price elasticity between S1, S2, and S3 to price each correctly

categories.name: Healthy Revenue Growth
ideas: Targeted advertising to increase customer base
Expand into other niches: men's and children's movies
Encourage S2 and S3 customers to mail more than one movie together to reduce per-shipment cost

categories.name: Cost Rationalization
ideas: Negotiate volume discounts with distributors to decrease distribution (mailing) cost
Negotiate with movie studios to reduce DVD purchase/amortization cost
Promote rentals of older movies with lower content amortization cost (already fully amortized)

recommendation: Chickflix has grown revenues by adding customers in S1 and S2, but has subsidized S1 with proceeds from S2 and S3 because S1 earns negative gross margins.
Chickflix must restructure S1 to return it to profitability — either by raising the subscription price (target ~$15/month) or by adding usage caps to limit the variable cost per subscriber.

Chickflix should rationalize costs by focusing on the two main variable cost drivers: distribution (mailing) cost and content amortization — through renegotiated contracts with distributors and movie studios.
Moving forward, Chickflix should evaluate entering other market niches (e.g., men's and children's movies) to diversify revenue and spread fixed costs.
risks: Raising S1 prices could lead to customer churn or cannibalization — customers from S2 switching to a repriced S1, or S1 customers leaving entirely.
Chickflix must identify the premium/differentiated offering of S2 and S3 before repricing to avoid commodity perception.
Aggressive growth in S1 may continue to erode margins if cost structure is not addressed first.
next_steps: Analyze customers' price elasticity for each subscription type before adjusting prices
Renegotiate contracts with distributors and movie studios to reduce per-rental variable cost
Model the customer retention impact of various S1 price points against the margin improvement
